# Problem Statement

## Market Perspective

Mainframes still run the show for banks, insurers, healthcare systems, and government agencies. Most of the world's high-value transactions touch a mainframe at some point. That isn't changing anytime soon. What is changing is that organizations are starting to deploy autonomous AI agents on these platforms to handle complex workflows, and every new agent-to-agent interaction is a potential entry point for unauthorized access, data theft, or lateral movement. Nobody has built a security solution that enforces trust at the level of individual agent communications within mainframe topologies.

Here's the pain point. The security models we have for mainframe workloads were designed around humans logging into sessions, not machines talking to other machines at high frequency. Security teams end up bolting perimeter-based controls or static credentials onto agent architectures, which creates gaps. A compromised or misbehaving agent can operate in those gaps without anyone noticing. Organizations are stuck choosing between slowing down agent adoption to keep their security posture intact or accepting more risk to get the operational benefits of automation.

There's a real market opportunity in building a mainframe-native trust fabric that kills this trade-off. If you can continuously validate agent identity, authorization, and behavioral integrity on every interaction without adding prohibitive latency, you unlock confident scaling of autonomous agent deployments in the most security-sensitive computing environments on earth.

## Industry Perspective

Zero-trust security has gained serious traction in distributed cloud and network environments. NIST published SP 800-207, major cloud providers have shipped their own implementations, and "never trust, always verify" is an accepted architectural principle at this point. But applying zero-trust to autonomous agent ecosystems on mainframe platforms? That's mostly uncharted territory. The zero-trust implementations that exist today focus on user-to-application or service-to-service communication patterns. They don't account for the specific execution domains you find on mainframes: LPARs, address spaces, AI accelerator domains, container runtimes, all coexisting under a single sysplex.

Agent orchestration efforts and multi-agent system research have focused heavily on functional coordination, task decomposition, and output quality. Security gets treated as an infrastructure problem that the hosting platform should handle. This creates a fundamental gap. Agent frameworks assume they're running in a trusted environment. Meanwhile, mainframe security subsystems like RACF were never designed to evaluate the dynamic, context-dependent trust requirements of autonomous agent interactions. Nobody has built a system that pulls together RACF permissions, workload classifications, data sensitivity labels, and runtime attestation into a single per-interaction trust evaluation for agents.

The limitations are pretty concrete. Static API keys and service accounts give persistent access regardless of what an agent is actually doing at runtime. Anomaly detection systems work at the network or application layer but can't see agent-level intent or authorization context. Audit trails record authentication events but not the trust reasoning behind individual agent-to-agent calls, so when compliance or forensic teams need to investigate an incident in an agent-heavy environment, they don't have the granularity they need.

## Legal & Compliance Perspective

Regulatory frameworks are converging on requirements that directly affect how autonomous agents need to be governed. The EU AI Act requires transparency, traceability, and human oversight for high-risk AI systems, and that includes AI operating in critical infrastructure like financial services mainframes. In the US, guidance from the OCC, FFIEC, and SEC increasingly expects financial institutions to show continuous monitoring and auditability of automated systems that touch sensitive data. These regulations assume that organizations can attribute actions to specific agents, validate authorization in real time, and produce thorough audit trails. Most mainframe agent deployments today can't reliably do any of that.

Data protection regulations (GDPR, CCPA, and sector-specific rules like HIPAA and PCI DSS) impose strict requirements on how sensitive data gets accessed and by what identity. When autonomous agents interact across workload boundaries on a mainframe, each data access has to be justified, logged, and limited to the minimum scope necessary. Without a trust fabric that checks data sensitivity labels and enforces least-privilege at the agent interaction level, organizations risk non-compliance through over-permissioned agents accessing data beyond what they actually need. That risk scales directly with the number of agents deployed and how much autonomy they have.

Speed and volume make the compliance challenge worse. Traditional audit approaches that rely on periodic review of access logs just don't work when thousands of agent interactions happen every second. Regulators and internal risk teams want continuous, automated assurance that every agent interaction was authorized, contextually appropriate, and traceable to a trust decision. Without a system that delivers this, any organization running autonomous agents on mainframe infrastructure carries material regulatory exposure.

## Core Problem

Autonomous agents on mainframes today inherit static trust from the infrastructure around them. There is no mechanism to continuously validate identity, authorization, execution context, and behavioral integrity at the level of individual agent-to-agent interactions. This means organizations can't prevent lateral movement by compromised agents, can't enforce least-privilege access across different mainframe execution domains, and can't produce the per-interaction audit trails that modern regulatory frameworks demand. What we need is a mainframe-native zero-trust fabric that dynamically evaluates and enforces trust for every agent communication, pulling security context from existing mainframe security subsystems, workload metadata, and runtime attestation to make real-time trust decisions.

# Technical Implementation

## Invention Summary

### Core Novelty
The Zero-Trust Agent Fabric introduces a trust evaluation layer built natively for mainframes that governs all autonomous agent-to-agent communication. It works by dynamically computing trust scores from RACF permissions, workload classifications, data sensitivity labels, and runtime attestations. Traditional perimeter-based security models grant static trust based on where something sits in the infrastructure. This fabric does something different: it validates trust on every single interaction, with continuous re-evaluation throughout the lifecycle of each agent operation. The system creates a unified trust plane that spans LPARs, containers, address spaces, and AI accelerator domains. As far as we can tell, this kind of topology-aware zero-trust model has no precedent in mainframe agent orchestration.

### Sequential Inventive Steps
1. **Step 1 - Multi-Domain Agent Identity Resolution**: The fabric discovers and catalogues all autonomous agents executing across different mainframe domains (LPARs, containers, z/OS address spaces, AI accelerator enclaves) and establishes cryptographically bound identity anchors for each one. These anchors incorporate the agent's RACF profile, execution environment fingerprint, and workload classification to produce a composite identity that can't be forged or transferred between domains.

2. **Step 2 - Dynamic Security Challenge Protocol**: Before any agent-to-agent invocation goes through, the fabric generates a context-sensitive security challenge tailored to the requesting agent's domain type and how sensitive the target interaction is. Challenges validate four dimensions at once: current identity freshness, authorization scope for the specific operation, execution environment integrity through attestation, and operational state consistency. Challenge parameters adapt based on the data sensitivity labels tied to the target agent's resources.

3. **Step 3 - Continuous Trust Score Computation and Decay**: The fabric keeps a real-time trust score for every active agent. This score comes from a weighted combination of successful challenge responses, behavioral consistency metrics, RACF permission alignment, and how fresh the environmental attestation is. Trust scores decay over time. They also degrade immediately if the system detects anomalous patterns like unusual invocation frequencies, out-of-scope data access attempts, or environment drift. The decay model means that even agents with a strong track record have to continuously demonstrate they're still trustworthy.

4. **Step 4 - Automated Restriction and Quarantine Enforcement**: When an agent's trust score drops below configurable thresholds, the fabric automatically applies graduated enforcement actions, from communication throttling all the way to full quarantine. Quarantined agents get isolated from the fabric's communication plane, but their state is preserved for forensic analysis. Every trust decision, score transition, and enforcement action goes into an immutable audit trail that plugs into existing mainframe security auditing infrastructure.

### Additional Claims
- **Claim 1**: A method for cross-domain trust federation where agents operating in different mainframe isolation domains (for example, an LPAR-resident agent communicating with a container-resident agent) must satisfy domain-bridging trust requirements. These requirements account for the differing security properties of each execution environment. The fabric applies the stricter security posture of the two domains as the baseline for trust evaluation.

- **Claim 2**: A system for trust-aware agent workflow orchestration where multi-step agent workflows are pre-validated against projected trust requirements. The fabric proactively identifies steps where trust scores may be insufficient, allowing preemptive re-attestation or workflow rerouting to higher-trust agent instances before execution begins.

### Value to IBM
IBM's z/OS mainframe platform is still the backbone of mission-critical computing for financial institutions, government agencies, and large enterprises. As those organizations adopt autonomous AI agents to automate mainframe operations, the security model has to move beyond traditional RACF-based access control to deal with the specific risks of agent-to-agent lateral movement. The Zero-Trust Agent Fabric positions IBM as the leader in secure agentic computing on mainframes. This is a differentiation point that competing platforms can't easily replicate because IBM has unique integration of RACF, workload management, and hardware-level attestation capabilities.

This invention supports IBM's strategy of embedding AI deep into the mainframe ecosystem while maintaining the security guarantees customers depend on. By making zero-trust agent governance a native capability of the mainframe fabric rather than something bolted on after the fact, IBM can capture the emerging market for enterprise agent orchestration platforms. Organizations that already trust IBM mainframes for their most sensitive workloads get a natural upgrade path to agentic automation without giving up their security posture. That reinforces mainframe relevance and drives new software licensing revenue.

## Implementation

### Primary Approach
The Zero-Trust Agent Fabric runs as a system-level service within z/OS. It intercepts all inter-agent communication using a combination of SVC (Supervisor Call) hooks and cross-memory service interception points. Every agent registers with the fabric when it starts up, providing its execution context, RACF identity, workload classification, and an initial environment attestation. The fabric maintains an in-memory trust graph that maps all registered agents along with their current trust scores, updated in real time as interactions happen.

When Agent A tries to invoke Agent B, the fabric intercepts the request before any data changes hands. It first resolves both agents' composite identities, then builds a security challenge appropriate to the sensitivity level of the interaction. The challenge is a multi-factor validation that checks several things at once: a cryptographic proof of identity freshness (to prevent replay of stale credentials), a scope verification against RACF profiles for the specific operation, an environment attestation check using hardware-rooted trust (taking advantage of z/OS Crypto Express capabilities where available), and a behavioral consistency check against the agent's historical operational patterns.

Trust scores are floating-point values between 0.0 and 1.0. A weighted scoring engine computes them. The weights are configurable per installation so they can reflect whatever security policies the organization has in place. Scores decay according to a configurable half-life model; an agent that's been idle for a while will naturally need to re-attest before it can resume high-sensitivity communications. Anomaly detection feeds into the scoring engine through a behavioral analysis component that tracks invocation patterns, data volume transfers, and timing characteristics.

#### Code Example
```python
class TrustScore:
    def __init__(self, agent_id, initial_score=0.0):
        self.agent_id = agent_id
        self.score = initial_score
        self.last_attestation = None
        self.decay_half_life_seconds = 300
        self.dimension_weights = {
            "identity": 0.30,
            "authorization": 0.25,
            "environment": 0.25,
            "behavior": 0.20
        }

    def compute(self, challenge_results, elapsed_since_attestation):
        weighted_sum = sum(
            self.dimension_weights[dim] * challenge_results.get(dim, 0.0)
            for dim in self.dimension_weights
        )
        decay_factor = 0.5 ** (elapsed_since_attestation / self.decay_half_life_seconds)
        self.score = weighted_sum * decay_factor
        return self.score


class ZeroTrustFabric:
    def __init__(self, racf_connector, attestation_service, audit_logger):
        self.racf = racf_connector
        self.attestation = attestation_service
        self.audit = audit_logger
        self.trust_scores = {}
        self.quarantined_agents = set()
        self.thresholds = {
            "allow": 0.75,
            "throttle": 0.50,
            "quarantine": 0.25
        }

    def register_agent(self, agent_id, execution_domain, workload_class):
        env_attestation = self.attestation.attest(agent_id, execution_domain)
        racf_profile = self.racf.resolve_profile(agent_id)
        initial_results = {
            "identity": 1.0 if racf_profile.is_valid else 0.0,
            "authorization": 1.0,
            "environment": env_attestation.confidence,
            "behavior": 0.5
        }
        score = TrustScore(agent_id)
        score.compute(initial_results, elapsed_since_attestation=0)
        self.trust_scores[agent_id] = score
        self.audit.log("REGISTER", agent_id, score.score, execution_domain)
        return score.score

    def evaluate_interaction(self, source_agent, target_agent, operation):
        if source_agent in self.quarantined_agents:
            self.audit.log("DENIED_QUARANTINED", source_agent, 0.0, operation)
            return False

        challenge = self._build_challenge(source_agent, target_agent, operation)
        challenge_results = self._execute_challenge(source_agent, challenge)

        source_score = self.trust_scores[source_agent]
        elapsed = self._seconds_since_last_attestation(source_agent)
        current_trust = source_score.compute(challenge_results, elapsed)

        enforcement = self._determine_enforcement(current_trust)
        self.audit.log("EVALUATE", source_agent, current_trust, operation, enforcement)

        if enforcement == "quarantine":
            self.quarantined_agents.add(source_agent)
            return False
        if enforcement == "throttle":
            self._apply_rate_limit(source_agent)
        return enforcement in ("allow", "throttle")

    def _build_challenge(self, source, target, operation):
        sensitivity = self._get_data_sensitivity(target, operation)
        challenge_factors = ["identity_proof", "racf_scope_check"]
        if sensitivity in ("confidential", "restricted"):
            challenge_factors.append("hardware_attestation")
            challenge_factors.append("behavioral_consistency")
        return {"factors": challenge_factors, "sensitivity": sensitivity}

    def _execute_challenge(self, agent_id, challenge):
        results = {}
        for factor in challenge["factors"]:
            if factor == "identity_proof":
                results["identity"] = self._verify_identity_freshness(agent_id)
            elif factor == "racf_scope_check":
                results["authorization"] = self._verify_racf_scope(agent_id)
            elif factor == "hardware_attestation":
                results["environment"] = self.attestation.verify(agent_id)
            elif factor == "behavioral_consistency":
                results["behavior"] = self._check_behavioral_baseline(agent_id)
        return results

    def _determine_enforcement(self, trust_value):
        if trust_value >= self.thresholds["allow"]:
            return "allow"
        if trust_value >= self.thresholds["throttle"]:
            return "throttle"
        if trust_value >= self.thresholds["quarantine"]:
            return "deny"
        return "quarantine"
```

The `ZeroTrustFabric` class is the central governance layer. When `evaluate_interaction` gets called, it builds a challenge whose complexity scales with how sensitive the target operation's data is. `TrustScore` applies time-based decay so agents can't coast on a single successful attestation indefinitely. The key insight with the enforcement logic is graduated responses: agents with moderately degraded trust get throttled rather than immediately blocked. This gives you operational resilience while still clamping down on risk. The audit logger captures every trust decision with full context, which means security teams can reconstruct the complete chain of trust evaluations for any agent interaction after the fact.

### Alternative Approaches

#### Alternative 1: Blockchain-Anchored Trust Ledger
Instead of keeping trust scores in an in-memory graph managed by the fabric service, we could record each trust evaluation and score transition to a permissioned blockchain running inside the mainframe environment. Agent trust histories would become immutable and independently verifiable by any participant in the fabric. This approach trades computational overhead and latency for stronger tamper resistance and decentralized trust verification. It would be particularly useful in multi-tenant mainframe environments where different organizations share infrastructure but don't fully trust each other's security administration. The blockchain consensus mechanism could be optimized for the low-latency, high-throughput demands of mainframe workloads using a Byzantine fault tolerant protocol adapted for the predictable network topology within a single physical system.

#### Alternative 2: Federated Trust Mesh Across Sysplex Clusters
Rather than running a single centralized fabric instance, we could implement the zero-trust architecture as a federated mesh. Each LPAR or system within a Parallel Sysplex would operate its own trust evaluation engine. These engines would synchronize trust scores and policy updates through the Sysplex coupling facility, so trust decisions can be made locally for low-latency enforcement while still maintaining global consistency across the cluster. This approach scales naturally as the Sysplex grows and avoids a single point of failure in the trust infrastructure. For cross-system agent invocations, both the source and target system's local trust engines would need to endorse the interaction, which implements a form of mutual trust validation that strengthens the overall security posture.

## Embodiments

### Embodiment 1: Financial Transaction Processing with AI Agents
A large bank runs a z/OS mainframe with autonomous AI agents handling real-time fraud detection, transaction routing, and regulatory compliance checking. A fraud detection agent in LPAR-A spots a suspicious transaction pattern and needs to call a compliance checking agent running in a container on zCX (z/OS Container Extensions) to figure out whether a Suspicious Activity Report needs to be filed.

The Zero-Trust Agent Fabric intercepts this cross-domain invocation. Because the interaction involves restricted financial data, the fabric issues a full four-factor challenge. It verifies the fraud detection agent's RACF identity hasn't been modified since the last attestation. It confirms the agent's authorization scope includes SAR-related data access. It validates the container environment's integrity through a hardware-rooted attestation using the Crypto Express adapter. And it checks that the agent's invocation pattern looks consistent with its historical behavior during fraud detection workflows. The compliance agent's trust score gets evaluated too, to make sure it hasn't been compromised. Both agents pass with trust scores above 0.85, and the interaction proceeds with full audit logging.

Later that day, a monitoring agent starts behaving strangely, attempting to access customer PII outside its normal operational pattern. Its behavioral consistency score drops, the overall trust score falls below 0.50, and the fabric automatically throttles its communications while sending an alert to the security operations team.

### Embodiment 2: Hybrid Cloud Agent Orchestration for Insurance Claims
An insurance company uses IBM z/OS mainframes integrated with IBM Cloud to process claims through a pipeline of specialized AI agents. A claims intake agent on the mainframe receives a new claim and needs to coordinate with an image analysis agent running on an AI accelerator (IBM Telum processor) and a policy verification agent in a separate LPAR. The Zero-Trust Agent Fabric manages trust across all three execution domains.

The intake agent's trust score reflects its RACF permissions for claims data, its attestation within the mainframe address space, and its consistent behavioral pattern of sequential claim processing. When it invokes the AI accelerator-based image analysis agent, the fabric recognizes the domain transition and applies enhanced attestation requirements that validate the accelerator environment's firmware integrity. The image analysis agent returns damage assessment results with a data sensitivity label of "confidential," and the fabric uses that label to enforce stricter trust requirements on the subsequent call to the policy verification agent.

If the company later deploys additional agents to handle surge capacity during a natural disaster, each new agent has to establish trust from scratch through the fabric's registration process. No compromised or misconfigured agent can inherit trust from the broader infrastructure. The complete audit trail lets the company show regulators that every agent interaction in the claims pipeline was individually authorized and continuously validated.

## Implementation

### Primary Approach
The Zero-Trust Agent Fabric operates as a system-level service within z/OS that intercepts all inter-agent communication through a combination of SVC (Supervisor Call) hooks and cross-memory service interception points. Every agent registers with the fabric upon initialization, providing its execution context, RACF identity, workload classification, and an initial environment attestation. The fabric maintains an in-memory trust graph that maps all registered agents and their current trust scores, updated in real time as interactions occur.

When Agent A attempts to invoke Agent B, the request is intercepted by the fabric before any data exchange occurs. The fabric first resolves both agents' composite identities, then constructs a security challenge appropriate to the interaction's sensitivity level. The challenge is a multi-factor validation that combines a cryptographic proof of identity freshness (preventing replay of stale credentials), a scope verification against RACF profiles for the specific operation, an environment attestation check using hardware-rooted trust (leveraging z/OS Crypto Express capabilities where available), and a behavioral consistency check against the agent's historical operational patterns.

Trust scores are represented as floating-point values between 0.0 and 1.0, computed by a weighted scoring engine. The weights are configurable per installation and can reflect organizational security policies. Scores decay according to a configurable half-life model, meaning that an agent idle for a period will naturally require re-attestation before resuming high-sensitivity communications. Anomaly detection feeds into the scoring engine through a behavioral analysis component that tracks invocation patterns, data volume transfers, and timing characteristics.

class TrustScore:
    def __init__(self, agent_id, initial_score=0.0):
        self.agent_id = agent_id
        self.score = initial_score
        self.last_attestation = None
        self.decay_half_life_seconds = 300
        self.dimension_weights = {
            "identity": 0.30,
            "authorization": 0.25,
            "environment": 0.25,
            "behavior": 0.20
        }

    def compute(self, challenge_results, elapsed_since_attestation):
        weighted_sum = sum(
            self.dimension_weights[dim] * challenge_results.get(dim, 0.0)
            for dim in self.dimension_weights
        )
        decay_factor = 0.5 ** (elapsed_since_attestation / self.decay_half_life_seconds)
        self.score = weighted_sum * decay_factor
        return self.score

    def __init__(self, racf_connector, attestation_service, audit_logger):
        self.racf = racf_connector
        self.attestation = attestation_service
        self.audit = audit_logger
        self.trust_scores = {}
        self.quarantined_agents = set()
        self.thresholds = {
            "allow": 0.75,
            "throttle": 0.50,
            "quarantine": 0.25
        }

    def register_agent(self, agent_id, execution_domain, workload_class):
        env_attestation = self.attestation.attest(agent_id, execution_domain)
        racf_profile = self.racf.resolve_profile(agent_id)
        initial_results = {
            "identity": 1.0 if racf_profile.is_valid else 0.0,
            "authorization": 1.0,
            "environment": env_attestation.confidence,
            "behavior": 0.5
        }
        score = TrustScore(agent_id)
        score.compute(initial_results, elapsed_since_attestation=0)
        self.trust_scores[agent_id] = score
        self.audit.log("REGISTER", agent_id, score.score, execution_domain)
        return score.score

    def evaluate_interaction(self, source_agent, target_agent, operation):
        if source_agent in self.quarantined_agents:
            self.audit.log("DENIED_QUARANTINED", source_agent, 0.0, operation)
            return False

        challenge = self._build_challenge(source_agent, target_agent, operation)
        challenge_results = self._execute_challenge(source_agent, challenge)

        source_score = self.trust_scores[source_agent]
        elapsed = self._seconds_since_last_attestation(source_agent)
        current_trust = source_score.compute(challenge_results, elapsed)

        enforcement = self._determine_enforcement(current_trust)
        self.audit.log("EVALUATE", source_agent, current_trust, operation, enforcement)

        if enforcement == "quarantine":
            self.quarantined_agents.add(source_agent)
            return False
        if enforcement == "throttle":
            self._apply_rate_limit(source_agent)
        return enforcement in ("allow", "throttle")

    def _build_challenge(self, source, target, operation):
        sensitivity = self._get_data_sensitivity(target, operation)
        challenge_factors = ["identity_proof", "racf_scope_check"]
        if sensitivity in ("confidential", "restricted"):
            challenge_factors.append("hardware_attestation")
            challenge_factors.append("behavioral_consistency")
        return {"factors": challenge_factors, "sensitivity": sensitivity}

    def _execute_challenge(self, agent_id, challenge):
        results = {}
        for factor in challenge["factors"]:
            if factor == "identity_proof":
                results["identity"] = self._verify_identity_freshness(agent_id)
            elif factor == "racf_scope_check":
                results["authorization"] = self._verify_racf_scope(agent_id)
            elif factor == "hardware_attestation":
                results["environment"] = self.attestation.verify(agent_id)
            elif factor == "behavioral_consistency":
                results["behavior"] = self._check_behavioral_baseline(agent_id)
        return results

    def _determine_enforcement(self, trust_value):
        if trust_value >= self.thresholds["allow"]:
            return "allow"
        if trust_value >= self.thresholds["throttle"]:
            return "throttle"
        if trust_value >= self.thresholds["quarantine"]:
            return "deny"
        return "quarantine"
